Harangue

huh-RANG · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Harangue is a lengthy, aggressive speech of criticism or lecture delivered at its listeners.

The customer launched into a ten-minute harangue about the delayed flight.

Worked Example

The coach's postgame harangue lasted nearly twenty minutes, covering every mistake the team had made that season.

A long, forceful, one-sided speech of criticism -- not a quick word -- is exactly what a harangue is.

Antonyms

compliment

tribute

tribute: a statement of respect or admiration

How Strong Is It? — complaint → harangue → tirade

complaint vs. harangue

complaint vs. harangue: A complaint can be brief; a harangue is a long, forceful, aggressive speech of criticism.

tirade vs. harangue

tirade vs. harangue: Tirade is close to harangue in intensity, though it can be even more emotionally out-of-control and less structured.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Harangue traces back through French to a Germanic root related to a public 'ring' or assembly -- the same imagined circle of listeners a harangue is delivered to.

Use the root in a new word: ring

Use the root in a new word: ring: In its oldest recorded sense, the Germanic root behind harangue referred to a circle or assembly of people -- the same word family that gives us 'ring.'
